Giving Wellness a Face

The Wellness Picture turns SonderMind's clinical wellness methodology into something clients can see: six areas of wellness, each described on a supportive scale from Needs Care to Flourishing. I led design and research for the client experience, from the concept study to a rollout plan designed to validate the methodology without putting vulnerable clients at risk.

My role

Design and research owner
Product design, UX research, launch strategy

Team

Product, engineering, applied science, and clinical leadership

Status

Framework validated in a concept study; rollout planned, not launched

context

Rich data on every client, and none of it shown back

SonderMind already held rich data on its clients, from session transcripts and reflections to mood logs and AI Coach conversations, and showed none of it back to them. Clients experienced the app as a set of disconnected tools with no through-line, and providers had only lagging symptom scores. Leadership wanted outcomes to become a core platform capability, not a one-off feature, and the Wellness Picture was the first place it would show up. The bet was different for each group:

FOR SONDERMINDOutcomes it could report, and a reason to choose it

A shared wellness measure to report outcomes beyond symptom scores, and a clinical methodology clients can actually see, setting the platform apart from symptom-checklist care.

FOR CLIENTSA reason to come back

One picture that ties the self-care tools together, meant to lift engagement with those tools and everyday use of the app, and retention for therapy clients.

FOR PROVIDERSContext between sessions

Insight into what sits behind a client’s symptoms, which only pays off if clinicians adopt it and bring it into care.

SonderMind's clinicians developed a new methodology for measuring wellness. Instead of tracking symptoms alone, through questionnaires like the PHQ-9 and GAD-7, it looks across six areas using user-provided input from care tools: Emotional, Social, Physical, Cognitive, Environmental, and Spiritual. The scores were already being calculated behind the scenes, but that picture lived in the clinical model, not in anything clients could look at.

EmotionalHandling feelings and stress
SocialConnection, support, belonging
PhysicalRest, movement, food
CognitiveFocus and curiosity, not IQ
EnvironmentalHome, work, surroundings
SpiritualPurpose and values, not religion

A ladder instead of a score

The Wellness Picture gives each area a state on a five-step scale, Needs Care, Emerging, Growing, Thriving, Flourishing, with plain-language copy about what that state feels like. It's meant to read as a reflection, not a grade.

Emotional scale overview

Flourishing

Emotions are information, not disruption

You move through hard feelings without losing yourself in them, and you recover faster than you used to. You know yourself well enough that not much catches you completely off guard.

process

Three decisions that shaped it

DECISION 1Prove it before we sell it

The free release had to pass three gates before anything was built on top: do people want it, will they trust it, and is there enough data to be fair.

DECISION 2Change the method where people would misread it

A new name, a five-step ladder of words instead of 0–1 scores, good signs counting as much as bad ones, and a validated “Needs Care” cutoff.

DECISION 3Design and launch for harm

Six rules for an AI that can be wrong, and a launch re-scoped to therapy clients first, with harm signals that can stop it.

Testing the framework with strangers first

I ran an unmoderated concept study with 20 participants who were in therapy or using wellness and self-care apps. All 20 said the six areas felt like a complete picture of wellness, and all 20 understood the scale.

20/20said the six areas felt like a complete picture
20/20understood the five-step scale
17/20wanted updates over time, not just once
0/20called the wording judgmental

Small copy decisions did a lot of the work. Pairing each area with a one-line explanation, like “values, sense of purpose, inner peace” for Spiritual, kept people from misreading the labels. Some participants liked letter grades because they felt concrete, but grades conflict with the clinical principles behind the product, so we kept descriptive states.

Why I didn’t trust it yet

When 20 out of 20 agree, you may be measuring how polite a paid panel is. Only 8 of the 20 were in therapy, and 17 had never used SonderMind. It was a good signal, not proof.

Three directions, one carried forward

Alongside the framework, I tested three visual directions for the same content, as static mockups. Circle put every area on a card with a letter-grade ring. Square showed one area at a time as a single lotus on the five-step ladder. Heart told each area's story through an illustrated leaf and a short reflection. Square drew the most votes for its warmth and its focus on one area without feeling overwhelming, and it's the direction the product carried forward.

Then asking who it could hurt

Provider interviews raised a question the study hadn't been read for: could the clients most eager to see their picture be the ones least able to absorb a low reading? I re-analyzed all 20 responses against that question and built a persona framework from them.

Sorting the 20 participants on two questions, not one: do they want to see it, and can they handle a low reading?

Can handle a low readingHurt by a low readingWants to see it
9 + 5 peopleThe Observer and the Realist

Like knowing where they stand. A low reading is just information.

4 people · highest riskThe Self-Judger

Wants it badly and is hurt by what they find. 3 of 4 asked for weekly updates.

Doesn't want it
0 peopleNot found in this study

A survey people sign up for can't find people who don't care.

2 peopleThe Avoider

Would rather not be told. Needs an easy way out.

Risk 01 · How a client reads itThe ladder becomes a verdict

Many clients would read any step below the top as a statement about who they are, not where they are right now.

Risk 02 · What seeing it doesThe app creates the worry

Some clients feel fine until they see a low reading. Then the app has handed them a worry they didn’t have.

The answer changed the brief. 18 of 20 wanted to see where they landed, so appetite barely told people apart; resilience did, and nothing in the product can see it. The most self-critical participants were among the most eager, so making the feature opt-in doesn't protect them. Every design choice had to be safe for the most vulnerable reader, not the average one, and notification cadence defaults to conservative.

A launch built to validate it

The data shaped the plan as much as the risk did. Early on, I raised that we needed to know the data thresholds before deciding who would see a picture, and talked through what was ethically okay to show for how much data we had. We didn’t want to show anyone a picture we weren’t sure of. I worked closely with our data analyst, who pulled the numbers against those thresholds: who would get a picture at all, and how many clients would have all six areas filled in, just one or two, or none. Of roughly 3,000 eligible users, only a few hundred had enough activity for a meaningful picture, and most would see only some of the six areas filled in. A cohort of about 300 couldn’t prove anything statistically, so the rollout couldn’t be a classic A/B test. Each phase had to be a safety and comprehension gate, with a permanent holdback for outcomes.

I wrote the rollout plan around harm rather than engagement. It proposed:

  • A phased rollout behind a feature flag, with each phase gated on safety and comprehension signals
  • A permanent holdback group, so outcomes can actually be compared against something
  • Automatic rollback triggers, like a label that flips two states with no new data
  • Treating score improvement as a goal, not a success metric, so there's no pressure to make scores move
outcome

Where it stands

The framework, the scale, and the supportive tone held up in the concept study, and the rollout plan was ready for review. My role ended in a company-wide layoff before the feature launched, so this preview covers the work through the study and the plan.

What changed because I was there

01 · STRATEGYI changed V1's job from "ship a feature" to "prove the method."

Premium and a therapist view were planned on top of a method nobody had seen. I set three gates the free version had to pass first: do people want it, will they trust it, and is there enough data to be fair?

02 · THE METHODI changed the clinical method where people would misread it.

I renamed it, replaced 0–1 scores with a five-step ladder, worked with the data scientist on scoring that could only pull people down, and made validating the "Needs Care" cutoff a launch requirement.

03 · RESPONSIBLE AII added an AI snapshot, and set the rules for an AI that can be wrong.

A short written read wasn't in the plan. I added one, reusing a summary agent from another project. Every reading shows where it came from, asks "does this feel right?", says it isn't a diagnosis, and stays quiet when data is thin.

04 · LAUNCHI rebuilt the launch around the people it could hurt.

A therapist showed me who a low reading would harm. With the PM and data scientist I re-scoped the rollout: therapy clients first, notifications on safe settings from day one, a holdout group, and harm signals that can stop it.
